g.text: DistanceFunc — chosen once, never branched on
int — tombstoned slots; the compaction signal
bool — stored vectors are unit length (Cosine)
bool — tombstone: dead as an answer, alive as a route

div.h3: How a node picks its top layer
div.p: Exponentially decaying: most nodes stop at layer 0, a few reach high. That is what makes the top sparse and the descent cheap. The RNG is seeded, so replaying the same inserts in the same order rebuilds an identical graph — which makes recovery-by-replay verifiable in a test.

g.text: A slot outlives its vector — delete AND update

div.p: Keeping the M nearest produces edges that all point into the same cluster, and searches strand in local minima.
Instead, drop candidate c when it already sits closer to an already-chosen neighbor s than to the node itself — you could reach c by hopping through s, so that edge buys nothing:
alpha = 1.0 classic HNSW heuristic alpha > 1.0 prunes harder, keeps more long-range shortcut edges, measurably lifts recall. Default 1.2.
Rejected candidates are backfilled if the list comes up short — a node with too few edges is a dead end during search.

div.h3: Delete(id) — a tombstone, never a removal
div.p: delete(ids, id) · deleted = true · numDeleted++ · re-elect the entry if this slot was the entry.

The slot keeps its index and every edge. It has to: slots are addressed by index, so removing one would shift every index above it and invalidate every neighbor list in the graph. And a node is a bridge — cut it out and a neighborhood nobody deleted becomes unreachable.
div.h3: Insert(id, v) on a live id — an upsert
div.p: Same three steps, then a brand-new slot is built for v with a fresh random level. The old slot is never edited in place: its inbound edges were chosen for the old vector, and pruning makes edges asymmetric, so finding them all is an O(N·M) scan of the whole graph.
Unchanged vector → early return, no slot spent. That is the WAL-replay path.
div.h3: What a tombstone costs until compaction
div.p: cands (the frontier) admits it — a dead node still bridges. results never does — a dead node is not an answer. So the search widens instead of returning fewer than k hits: 1.2× at 25% dead, 2.5× at 75%. pruneConnections demotes tombstones so they cannot evict a fresh live edge.
div.h3: Compact() — the only thing that gives the memory back
div.p: Builds a new graph over the live vectors and swaps it in whole. It cannot renumber the live one: neighbor lists are slot indices, so removing a slot invalidates every list in the graph at once.
Out comes exactly the graph you would have built if the dead vectors had never existed — same seeded RNG, same order — so it is testable by equality rather than by sampling recall.

Stop-the-world, and the pause tracks survivors: 2.6 s at 25% dead against 0.8 s at 75%, per 5k x 128. Compacting early costs more and reclaims less, so the index never self-triggers — callers poll Stats().DeadRatio() and pick the moment.
vector — dim × 4 bytes neighbors — up to 2M ints on L0 + M per upper layer at M=16: ≈ 256 B on L0, plus slice headers
16 KiB/vector → 1M vectors ≈ 16 GiB, graph overhead is noise
512 B/vector → the neighbor lists cost more than the data
Know which regime you are in — it decides whether quantization or graph compaction is the optimization that matters.
